topic: Forces and motion: Forces and braking
subject: physics

items.q: A driver sees a hazard, reacts, brakes, and brings the car safely to rest. Which distance is the stopping distance of the car?
items.correct: The thinking distance added to the braking distance travelled
items.misconception: The distance travelled after the brake pedal is pressed
items.why: Students picture stopping as beginning when the pedal is pressed, because that is the first moment something visibly happens to the car. The car is already moving towards the hazard during the driver's reaction time, and that thinking distance is part of the road used up.
items.random_wrong: Only the distance travelled while the brakes act

items.q: A car's speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?
items.correct: Thinking distance doubles and braking distance quadruples
items.misconception: Both the thinking distance and the braking distance double
items.why: Students apply the proportional reasoning that genuinely works for thinking distance to the braking distance as well. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so at twice the speed there is four times as much energy for the same braking force to remove.
items.random_wrong: Thinking distance is unchanged, braking distance doubles

items.q: Two identical lorries brake with the same braking force, one from 15 m/s and one from 25 m/s. Which statement about their stopping distances is correct?
items.correct: The lorry at 25 m/s needs the greater stopping distance
items.misconception: The 25 m/s lorry needs distance in proportion to speed
items.why: Students apply the proportional reasoning that genuinely works for thinking distance to the braking distance as well. Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so at twice the speed there is four times as much energy for the same braking force to remove.
items.random_wrong: The lorry at 15 m/s needs a greater distance in which to stop

items.q: (Physics only) A car is driven at 13 m/s, a typical speed in a built-up area. The driver's reaction time is about 0.7 s, and the braking distance at this speed is about 14 m. Estimate the distance the car needs to make an emergency stop.
items.correct: About 23 m: 9 m thinking, 14 m braking
items.misconception: About 14 m, which is the braking distance
items.why: Students picture stopping as beginning when the pedal is pressed, because that is the first moment something visibly happens to the car. The car is already moving towards the hazard during the driver's reaction time, and that thinking distance is part of the road used up.
items.random_wrong: About 9 m, covered while the driver reacts

items.q: (Physics only) A graph shows stopping distance on the vertical axis against speed on the horizontal axis for a family car. What shape is the line, and why?
items.correct: A curve that gets steeper, as braking distance grows fastest
items.misconception: A straight line through the origin, as distance = speed
items.why: Only the thinking distance contribution is a straight line, and students read that part as if it were the whole graph. Adding a curved braking distance term to a straight thinking distance term gives a total that curves upwards.
items.random_wrong: A straight line sloping steadily upward

items.q: (Physics only) Stopping distance is plotted against speed for a car and for a fully loaded lorry. At every speed shown the lorry's line lies above the car's line, and the gap between them widens as speed increases. What does the graph show?
items.correct: The lorry needs a longer stopping distance at every speed
items.misconception: The lorry driver has a longer reaction time than the car driver
items.why: The name suggests a property of the driver, and the reaction time really is fixed, so students transfer that fixedness to the distance. The reaction time is fixed, but the car covers more road during that same time when it is travelling faster.
items.random_wrong: The lorry is always driven faster than the car is driven

items.q: What does the specification say about human reaction times?
items.correct: They vary from person to person, typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s
items.misconception: They are the same for every driver, typically 0.7 s
items.why: Textbook questions usually quote a single value such as 0.7 s, which reads like a physical constant such as g. A quoted value is only a typical value. Real reaction times differ between people, and between trials for the same person.
items.random_wrong: They range from about 2 s to about 3 s for almost everyone

items.q: Five students measure their own reaction times and obtain 0.21 s, 0.34 s, 0.28 s, 0.52 s and 0.45 s. What is the best conclusion to draw?
items.correct: Reaction times differ between people, as expected
items.misconception: Four of the results must be wrong, as only one can be right
items.why: Textbook questions usually quote a single value such as 0.7 s, which reads like a physical constant such as g. A quoted value is only a typical value. Real reaction times differ between people, and between trials for the same person.
items.random_wrong: Everyone's reaction time is 0.36 s, the mean of the five

items.q: Which list contains only factors that the specification links to a driver's reaction time or ability to react?
items.correct: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions such as a phone
items.misconception: Tiredness, alcohol, icy roads and worn brake pads
items.why: Students know bad weather makes stopping worse, and attach it to whichever part of the stopping distance they meet first. Road conditions act on the braking distance through grip. They do not change how quickly the driver's brain and muscles respond.
items.random_wrong: Alcohol, drugs, heavy rain and under-inflated tyres

items.q: A driver holds a long hands-free phone conversation while driving. What does the specification say about this?
items.correct: Distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react
items.misconception: It has no effect, as the driver's hands stay on the wheel
items.why: Students learn tiredness, drugs and alcohol as the named list, and treat distractions as a separate and much softer category. The specification says distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react. A distracted driver reacts later, or does not react at all.
items.random_wrong: It lengthens the braking distance, not the thinking one

items.q: In the ruler drop test one student holds a ruler above a partner's open hand, releases it without warning, and the partner catches it as quickly as they can. Which measurement is taken, and what is done with it?
items.correct: The drop distance is measured, then converted to a time
items.misconception: The time in seconds is read directly from the ruler scale
items.why: The quantity actually measured is a length, and students report it as though the instrument had given a time. The ruler falls under gravity, so the drop distance must be converted to a time using a conversion chart or s = 1/2 g t2.
items.random_wrong: The number of centimetres is used as the time in seconds

items.q: A student's five ruler drop results convert to 0.18 s, 0.20 s, 0.19 s, 0.65 s and 0.21 s. How should the student's reaction time be reported?
items.correct: Discard 0.65 s and average the other four results
items.misconception: Average all five of the results to get about 0.29 s
items.why: Students are taught to repeat and average, but not to look at the values first, so anomalies are either kept or the whole set is abandoned for one favourite reading. Repeats are averaged, but a result that stands well clear of a tight cluster is an anomaly and should be left out of the mean.
items.random_wrong: Take the shortest result, 0.18 s, as the best attempt

items.q: At 20 m/s a rested driver has a thinking distance of 14 m, from a reaction time of 0.7 s. When tired, the same driver at the same speed has a thinking distance of 18 m. What does the data show?
items.correct: The tired driver's reaction time has risen to about 0.9 s
items.misconception: The reaction time has risen to about 2.5 s when tired
items.why: Two seconds feels short in everyday life, and the two-second rule for following distance is misremembered as a reaction time. The specification gives typical values of 0.2 s to 0.9 s; even a full second of reaction time would be unusually slow.
items.random_wrong: The reaction time is unchanged; the car was faster

items.q: Which pair of causes does the specification give for a longer braking distance?
items.correct: Wet or icy roads, and worn brakes or worn tyres
items.misconception: A worn-out engine and an ageing gearbox in the car
items.why: In everyday speech a car in poor condition means the whole vehicle, so students name whichever part they happen to know about. The specification limits poor condition of the vehicle to the brakes or the tyres, the two parts that act to slow the vehicle.
items.random_wrong: Fog and darkness, which hide the hazard ahead

items.q: A car is driven on an icy road at the same speed as it was on a dry road. Why is its braking distance longer on the ice?
items.correct: There is less grip, so a smaller braking force can act
items.misconception: The ice makes the vehicle heavier, so it takes far longer
items.why: Students know ice is dangerous but locate the cause inside the vehicle rather than at the contact between tyre and road. The brakes still work normally. What changes is the friction available where the tyres meet the road surface.
items.random_wrong: The brakes themselves stop working when the road is icy

items.q: A car has badly worn tyres. Which part of the stopping distance is increased, and why?
items.correct: The braking distance: the tyres grip the road less
items.misconception: The thinking distance, because the driver is more cautious
items.why: Students sort every factor into one undifferentiated pile of things that make stopping worse, without asking which stage of the stop it acts on. Brakes and tyres do nothing until the pedal is pressed, so they can only affect the distance travelled under the braking force.
items.random_wrong: The thinking distance, because tyres are part of the car

items.q: Heavy rain begins during a motorway journey. Which action best reflects the physics of stopping distance, and why?
items.correct: Slow down and leave a bigger gap, as braking needs more road
items.misconception: Keep the same gap, since the reaction time is unchanged
items.why: Textbook questions usually quote a single value such as 0.7 s, which reads like a physical constant such as g. A quoted value is only a typical value. Real reaction times differ between people, and between trials for the same person.
items.random_wrong: Brake as hard as possible each time, to stop sooner

items.q: On a dry road a car travelling at 31 m/s (about 70 mph) has a stopping distance of roughly 96 m, of which about 22 m is thinking distance. Estimate its stopping distance at the same speed on a wet road.
items.correct: About 170 m, since the braking part roughly doubles
items.misconception: About 96 m, because the driver reacts just as quickly
items.why: Textbook questions usually quote a single value such as 0.7 s, which reads like a physical constant such as g. A quoted value is only a typical value. Real reaction times differ between people, and between trials for the same person.
items.random_wrong: About 48 m, as water lubricates the road well

items.q: A force is applied to the brakes of a moving car. Which statement describes what happens to the energy?
items.correct: Friction does work, heating the brakes and slowing the car
items.misconception: Kinetic energy is destroyed by the friction in the brake pads
items.why: The car visibly stops, so the energy appears to have gone, and the phrase the brakes take the energy is half remembered. Energy is not destroyed. The friction force does work and energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, whose temperature rises.
items.random_wrong: Kinetic energy is stored in the brakes ready for later reuse

items.q: Two identical cars must each stop within the same distance, one from 12 m/s and the other from 24 m/s. Which needs the greater braking force, and why?
items.correct: The car at 24 m/s: more kinetic energy to remove
items.misconception: The car at 24 m/s needs less force, having more time
items.why: Students confuse stopping within a fixed distance with stopping over a longer distance, where a gentler force genuinely is enough. The distance is fixed by the question. Four times as much kinetic energy must be removed over that same distance, so the force must be greater.
items.random_wrong: The car at 12 m/s, as a slow car is harder to stop

items.q: A driver brakes very hard to avoid a collision, producing a very large deceleration. Why is this dangerous?
items.correct: A very large braking force is needed, risking loss of control
items.misconception: It is not dangerous, since stopping sooner is safer
items.why: Stopping sooner sounds unambiguously good, and students do not consider what the force needed does to the vehicle. The force needed can lock the wheels and make the vehicle skid, and repeated heavy braking overheats the brakes so they work less well.
items.random_wrong: A large deceleration always means a longer stopping distance

items.q: A lorry driver brakes heavily and repeatedly on a long, steep hill. What is the most likely consequence, and why?
items.correct: The brakes overheat, so they become less effective
items.misconception: The brakes cool down, as the lorry is slowing
items.why: The car visibly stops, so the energy appears to have gone, and the phrase the brakes take the energy is half remembered. Energy is not destroyed. The friction force does work and energy is transferred to the thermal store of the brakes, whose temperature rises.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic energy of the lorry rises as it descends

items.q: (HT only) A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 24 m/s brakes in an emergency and comes to rest in 3.0 s. Estimate the braking force acting on the car.
items.correct: 9600 N, from a = 8.0 m/s2 and then F = m a
items.misconception: 28 800 N, from the mass times the car's velocity
items.why: Both a mass and a velocity are printed in the question, so students reach for the two numbers in front of them rather than working out a first. A force needs an acceleration. Find a = change in velocity / time taken first, then use F = m a.
items.random_wrong: 3600 N, from mass x the 3.0 s stopping time

items.q: (HT only) A van of mass 2000 kg slows from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in 4.0 s while braking on a public road. Estimate the braking force acting on the van.
items.correct: 6000 N, from a deceleration of 3.0 m/s2
items.misconception: 9000 N, taking the change as the full 18 m/s
items.why: Almost every worked example ends with the vehicle at rest, so students learn the shortcut a = starting velocity / time and apply it without checking the final velocity. Acceleration is change in velocity / time. Subtract the final velocity from the initial one first; only when the vehicle stops is that the same as the starting velocity.
items.random_wrong: 36 000 N, from mass x the starting speed

items.q: Are the thinking distance and the braking distance always about the same size?
items.correct: No - braking distance grows much faster with speed and soon dominates.
items.misconception: The two parts are always roughly equal, so the stopping distance is about twice the thinking distance.
items.why: In the low-speed rows of the familiar Highway Code table the two columns look similar, and students generalise that coincidence. At 70 mph the braking distance is around three times the thinking distance, because it depends on speed squared.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.6.3 Forces and motion: Forces and braking
